                                   SUMMARY

     The  flammability    in microgravity    of three  U.S.-furnished     materials,   Delrin,  polymethylmethacrylate     (PMMA),
and  high-density    polyethylene,    was determined   using  a Russian-developed     combustion    tunnel  on Mir.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Four  4.5-ram-
diameter   cylindrical   samples  of each  plastic  were  ignited  under  concurrent    airflow   (in  the direction   of flame  spread)
with  velocities   from  no flow  to 8.5 cm/s.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
The  test  results  identify   a limiting   air-flow   velocity   Vh,"for each  material,
below  which  combustion    ceases.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Nominal   values   are V,,, <0.3  cm/s  for Delrin,   0.5 cm/s  for PMMA,  and  0.3  to
0.5 cm/s  for  polyethylene:   These  values  are lower  than  those  obtained   in prior  ground   testing.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Nevertheless,    they
demonstrate    that  flow  shutoff   is effective   for extinguishment     in the  microgravity   environment    of spacecraft.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Micro-
gravity   test  results  also show  that  the  plastic  materials   maintain   a stable  melt  ball  within  the  spreading   flame  zone.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
In general,   as the  concurrent   flow  velocity  V decreases,   the  flame-spread    rate  V, decreases,   from  an average   (for  all
three  materials)   ofV_: = 0.5-0.75  mm/s  at V = 8.5 cm/s  to V,: = 0.05-0.01  mm/s  at V = 0.3-0.5  cm/s.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Also,  as V
decreases,   the flames  become   less  visible  but  expand,   increasing   the  probability   of igniting  an adjacent   surface.

For  the  International   Space  Station,   the  probability    of  fire  is greater  than  for the  spacecraft   of previous   genera-
tions,  due  to the  higher  power  and  voltage   of the on-board   power  supplies  and  greater  volume  of scientific    instru-
mentation   with  high-temperature     operation.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Currently,    fire  safety  on Russian   spacecraft    is achieved  by prevention   methods   that exclude   the possibility   of
fire through   a wide  range  of different   means,  for example:

       •     selecting   structural   materials,   based  on the  results  of ground   testing,  with  priority  given  to
           materials   with  higher  limiting-oxygen     concentrations     for combustion      (C,,,,,) or/and   higher  oxygen    indices;
       •     specifying   nonflammable     materials   for the working  components    of the  electrical   systems;
       •    maintaining   low oxygen   concentrations     in the  spacecraft   pressurized   compartment    during   the launch
           phase:
       •    decreasing   the  vent  flow  locally   in the area  of the  electrical   components    that might  be potential   sources
           of  fire:
      •     eliminating    potential   sources   of structural   material   ignition  by methods   of current   protection   or by use  of
          nonflammable    instrumentation    and  cable  harnesses;   and
      •     preventing   flame  spread   to materials   that  are tlammable    in an oxygen-enriched    environment.

ABSTRACT (Maximum 200 words)

       The   flammability       in  microgravity      of  three   U.S.-furnished        materials,     Delrin,    polymethylmethacrylate        (PMMA),     and
        high-density      polyethylene,     was  determined     using   a Russian-developed        combustion      tunnel   on  Mir.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Four  4.5-mm-diameter
         cylindrical     samples    of  each   plastic   were   ignited   under   concurrent     airflow    (in  the  direction    of  flame   spread)    with   velocities
       from  no  flow   to  8.5  cm/s.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
The   test  results    identify    a limiting    air-flow    velocity    Vii m for  each   material,    below   which
       combustion      ceases.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Nominal     values   are  Vii m <0.3  cm/s   for  Deirin,    0.5  cm/s   for PMMA,    and  0.3  to  0.5  cm/s   for  polyethyl-
        ene.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text: These   values    are  lower   than   those   obtained     in  prior  ground    testing.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Nevertheless,      they  demonstrate       that  flow   shutoff
          is  effective     for  extinguishment        in  the  mierogravity      environment      of  spacecraft.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Microgravity       test  results    also  show   that   the
         plastic    materials    maintain    a stable   melt   ball  within    the  spreading    flame   zone.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
In  general,    as  the  concurrent     flow   velocity
     V  decreases,     the  flame-spread       rate V F decreases,    from   an  average    (for   all  three   materials)     of V F =  0.5-0.75   mm/s    at
     V = 8.5  cm/s   to V F = 0.05-0.01    mm/s    at V = 0.3-0.5    cm/s.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text:
Also,   as V decreases,     the  flames   become     less   visible   but
        expand,    increasing     the  probability     of  igniting   an  adjacent     surface.

Introduction:

A unique   environment     in which  flame  spreading,    a phenomenon     of fundamental,      scientific    interest,   has
importance    to  fire  safety   is that  of spacecraft    in which   the  gravitational     acceleration      is low  compared   with
that  of  the  Earth,   i.e., microgravity.

content.text:
Experiments    aboard  eight  Space  Shuttle   missions   between   October   1990
and  February   1995  were  conducted    using   the  Solid  Surface  Combustion    Experiment    (SSCE)  payload
apparatus    in an  effort  to determine    the mechanisms     of gas-phase    flame  spread   over  solid  fuel  surfaces    in the
absence   of any  buoyancy    induced    or externally   imposed    oxidizer   flow.

The  overall  SSCE  effort  began   in
December    of 1984.

0 2  / N 2 mixture   at a prescribed    pressure.

Five  of the  experiments    used  a thin  cellulosic    fuel,  ashless    filter
paper,  3 cm  wide  by  10 cm  long,  0.00825  cm half-thickness,     ignited   in five  different   ambient    conditions.

wide  by  2 cm  long,  0.32 cm half-thickness.

the  effect   of ambient    pressure   on flame  spread   over  the  thin  cellulosic    fuel  while   flights   STS 50 and  47 were
at the same  pressure    as two  of the  earlier   flights  but  at a lower  oxygen   concentration     in order  to  evaluate    the
effect   of ambient    oxygen    level  on  the  flame  spread   process   at microgravity.

Fire spread inside a spacecraft is a constant concern in space travel.

Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text: Twelve cylindrical samples of Delrin, PMMA, and high-density polyethylene were tested in microgravity aboard the Mir orbital station.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text: The paper reports limiting flow velocities of 0.5 cm/s for PMMA at 23.6% oxygen, 0.3 to 0.5 cm/s for polyethylene at 25.4% oxygen, and below 0.3 cm/s for Delrin at 25.4% oxygen.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text: The paper reports that after concurrent airflow was shut off, flame extinction in microgravity occurred within 5 to 20 seconds.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text: The paper reports that flame-spread rate decreased as concurrent airflow velocity decreased. It reports 0.5 to 0.75 mm/s at 8.5 cm/s airflow and 0.01 to 0.05 mm/s at 0.3 to 0.5 cm/s airflow.

source.title: Experimental Verification of Material Flammability in Space

content.text: The authors proposed continuing the space-experiment program using the Skorost and Skorost-M apparatus.

source.title: Determining the Cause of Reduced Concurrent Flame Spread over Thin Solid Fuels in Low Pressure and Low Gravity

content.text: The paper reports that experimental and numerical flame-spread rates decrease as ambient pressure decreases. The authors also report that finite-rate chemistry simulations underpredicted experimental spread rates at higher pressures and did not allow flame spread in lower-pressure environments.

source.title: Determining the Cause of Reduced Concurrent Flame Spread over Thin Solid Fuels in Low Pressure and Low Gravity

content.text: At 50 kPa, the FDS simulation using finite-rate chemistry showed only partial burning near the igniter. The flame blew off approximately 11 mm from the igniter, so no spread rate was determined for that condition.

source.title: Determining the Cause of Reduced Concurrent Flame Spread over Thin Solid Fuels in Low Pressure and Low Gravity

content.text: FDS simulations show that reducing ambient pressure or gravity level decreases average flame-spread rate. The paper reports that a pressure reduction to 33 kPa produces flame-spread rates similar to those observed in microgravity.

source.title: Determining the Cause of Reduced Concurrent Flame Spread over Thin Solid Fuels in Low Pressure and Low Gravity

content.text: The experiments and FDS simulations show decreasing pyrolysis length as ambient pressure and gravity level decrease. The authors report that pyrolysis length appears more sensitive to gravity changes than to pressure changes.

source.title: Determining the Cause of Reduced Concurrent Flame Spread over Thin Solid Fuels in Low Pressure and Low Gravity

content.text: FDS simulations at 100 kPa show a linear trend of decreasing flame-spread rate as gravity level decreases. The paper reports comparable flame-spread rates at lunar gravity (0.17g) and 46 kPa, and at Martian gravity (0.38g) and 54 kPa.

source.title: Solid Surface Combustion Experiment: Flame Spread in a Quiescent, Microgravity Environment

content.text: The paper analyzes Solid Surface Combustion Experiment data from eight Space Shuttle missions between October 1990 and February 1995. The experiments included thin cellulosic filter-paper fuels and thick PMMA samples in quiescent microgravity environments.

source.title: Solid Surface Combustion Experiment: Flame Spread in a Quiescent, Microgravity Environment

content.text: For thin cellulosic fuel, the paper reports an increase in experimental flame-spread rate with increasing ambient pressure. The radiation model agreed with experiments within 10%, while non-radiative models overpredicted spread rate by almost a factor of 2 to 3.

source.title: Solid Surface Combustion Experiment: Flame Spread in a Quiescent, Microgravity Environment

content.text: The authors report that flame size and hang distance were much larger in microgravity than in downward flame propagation under normal gravity.

source.title: Solid Surface Combustion Experiment: Flame Spread in a Quiescent, Microgravity Environment

content.text: For thick PMMA, the paper reports that experimental flame-spread rate decreased with distance. However, self-extinguishment was not observed in the experiments, possibly because the available fuel length was too short.

source.title: Solid Surface Combustion Experiment: Flame Spread in a Quiescent, Microgravity Environment

content.text: The authors report that their models indicate flame spread may decrease and eventually extinguish, even at high oxygen levels. This is a model result, not an observed experimental extinction in the reported tests.

source.title: Determining Flame Temperature By Broadband Two Color Pyrometry in A Flame Spreading Over A Thin Solid in Microgravity

content.text: The reported flame temperature remained relatively constant during the flame-spread process, averaging approximately 1305 K soon after ignition and throughout the test.

source.title: Determining Flame Temperature By Broadband Two Color Pyrometry in A Flame Spreading Over A Thin Solid in Microgravity

content.text: At the thermocouple measurement location, B2CP estimated approximately 1369 K, compared with 1426 K from the thermocouple after radiation and convection corrections. The authors describe the measurements as comparable within the error margin.

source.title: Determining Flame Temperature By Broadband Two Color Pyrometry in A Flame Spreading Over A Thin Solid in Microgravity

content.text: A Monte Carlo propagation analysis using a conservative 5% uncertainty in the green-to-red signal ratio produced an estimated temperature uncertainty of 117 K for the B2CP technique.

source.title: Determining Flame Temperature By Broadband Two Color Pyrometry in A Flame Spreading Over A Thin Solid in Microgravity

content.text: Image saturation prevented reliable temperature extraction near the flame center, the most luminous region. Values at those locations were artificially set to zero for plotting and must not be interpreted as measured zero temperatures.

source.title: Determining Flame Temperature By Broadband Two Color Pyrometry in A Flame Spreading Over A Thin Solid in Microgravity

content.text: The authors report validating the B2CP methodology using numerical simulations and experimental measurements of well-known coflow flames. They state that the technique provides an acceptable average temperature but is biased toward higher values.
